title: Alcohols, Ethers, Epoxides and Organometallics
description: Interconversion of oxygen functional groups, epoxide ring opening, and carbon–carbon bond formation with Grignard and organolithium reagents.
overview: Alcohols are the hub of functional-group chemistry. They are made from alkenes and carbonyl compounds, converted to halides and sulfonates for substitution and elimination, oxidized to aldehydes, ketones and acids, and dehydrated to alkenes. Ethers and epoxides are the relatives that share the C–O single bond. Organometallic reagents reverse the polarity of carbon and let us build new carbon skeletons, which is what makes synthesis possible.

This chapter covers the properties of alcohols, the ways to turn OH into a leaving group, oxidation, ethers and epoxides (including the regiochemistry of ring opening), and Grignard, organolithium and cuprate reagents.
objectives: Classify alcohols and explain their physical properties and acidity.
Convert alcohols to alkyl halides and sulfonates, with the stereochemistry of each method.
Choose the oxidant that gives an aldehyde, ketone or carboxylic acid.
Cleave ethers, and predict the regiochemistry of epoxide opening under acidic and basic conditions.
Prepare and use Grignard, organolithium and Gilman reagents, and plan alcohol syntheses from carbonyl compounds.

sections.title: Alcohols: properties and preparation
body: An **alcohol** has an OH group on an sp³ carbon. It is **primary**, **secondary** or **tertiary** according to the number of carbons on the carbinol carbon (one, two or three). The OH is polar and forms hydrogen bonds, so alcohols boil far higher than alkanes or ethers of similar mass and dissolve in water if small (methanol, ethanol, propanols are miscible). Alcohols are weak acids (pK_a 16–18, tertiary less acidic than methanol because bulky alkyl groups hinder solvation of the alkoxide) and weak bases (the conjugate acid, ROH₂⁺, has pK_a about −2). **Phenols**, with OH on an aromatic ring, are far more acidic (pK_a 10).
Alcohols can be made in many ways. The main routes are:

Carbonyl reduction is the most general. NaBH₄ in ethanol or methanol is mild and reduces aldehydes and ketones, but not esters or acids. LiAlH₄ in ether (followed by a careful aqueous workup) is much stronger and reduces all carbonyl groups, and it reacts violently with water.

sections.title: Converting OH into a leaving group
body: Hydroxide is a poor leaving group, so alcohols must be activated before they can be replaced.

list: **With HX.** Tertiary alcohols react with HCl or HBr by SN1 and secondary alcohols more slowly, and primary alcohols by SN2 with HBr or HI. Rearrangements are possible for SN1. The **Lucas test** distinguishes alcohol classes: ZnCl₂/conc. HCl turns a tertiary alcohol cloudy at once (insoluble R–Cl), a secondary alcohol in about 5 minutes, and a primary alcohol not at all at room temperature.

**With SOCl₂ or PBr₃.** **Thionyl chloride** (with pyridine) converts primary and secondary alcohols to chlorides, and PBr₃ gives bromides. Both proceed by SN2, with **inversion** and without rearrangement, and the by-products (SO₂, HCl) are gases.

**Sulfonate esters.** An alcohol treated with a sulfonyl chloride (TsCl, MsCl) and pyridine gives a **tosylate** or **mesylate**, a leaving group as good as bromide. The C–O bond is never broken, so the configuration of the carbon is **retained** during sulfonate formation. Subsequent SN2 with a nucleophile then inverts it.

**Mitsunobu reaction.** An alcohol, PPh₃ and DEAD (diethyl azodicarboxylate) activate the oxygen in situ, and an acidic pronucleophile (a carboxylic acid, phenol or imide) displaces it by SN2 with inversion. It converts a secondary alcohol to the inverted ester, azide or ether in one pot.

example.title: Stereochemistry through the sulfonate
example.problem: (R)-2-Octanol is treated with TsCl/pyridine and then with NaCN. Give the product configuration.
example.solution: TsCl converts the alcohol to the (R)-tosylate with retention. Cyanide displaces tosylate by SN2 with inversion, giving (S)-2-methyloctanenitrile. The overall change from alcohol to nitrile is therefore one inversion.

sections.title: Oxidation of alcohols
body: Oxidizing an alcohol removes the carbinol hydrogen along with the O–H hydrogen (net loss of two H, or addition of an O). A **primary** alcohol gives an aldehyde, which can go on to a carboxylic acid. A **secondary** alcohol gives a ketone. A **tertiary** alcohol has no carbinol hydrogen and is not oxidized.

head: Reagent
Primary alcohol gives
Secondary alcohol gives
Notes
rows: CrO₃, H₂SO₄, acetone (**Jones**) or Na₂Cr₂O₇, H₂SO₄
Aqueous acid: aldehyde hydrates and is further oxidized. Orange Cr(VI) turns green Cr(III).
table.caption: Alcohol oxidations.

body: With chromium(VI), the alcohol forms a chromate ester, and loss of the carbinol hydrogen by E2-like elimination expels Cr(IV). In water, an aldehyde adds water to form a hydrate, which oxidizes again; without water (PCC in CH₂Cl₂), the oxidation stops at the aldehyde. Chromium reagents are toxic, which is why the Swern and Dess–Martin methods are preferred in modern synthesis.

**Pinacol** (2,3-dimethylbutane-2,3-diol) is the model vicinal diol. In acid it rearranges to pinacolone (3,3-dimethylbutan-2-one) by loss of water to a cation and a methyl shift. Periodic acid (HIO₄ or NaIO₄) cleaves a 1,2-diol between the carbinol carbons to give two carbonyl compounds, a reaction used to analyze sugars.

sections.title: Ethers
body: An **ether** has an oxygen bonded to two carbons, R–O–R′. Ethers cannot hydrogen-bond to each other, so their boiling points are low (diethyl ether 35 °C), but their oxygen lone pairs accept hydrogen bonds, so they dissolve in water to some extent. They are inert to bases, nucleophiles, mild oxidants and reducing agents, which makes them ideal solvents: **diethyl ether**, **tetrahydrofuran (THF)** and dioxane. They also solvate cations by coordination, which is how they stabilize Grignard reagents.

Ethers are made by the Williamson synthesis (alkoxide plus primary alkyl halide) or by acid-catalyzed dehydration of two molecules of a primary alcohol, or by alkoxymercuration of an alkene. Their one useful reaction is **cleavage** by strong acids, HBr or HI: protonation of the oxygen, then SN2 attack by halide on the less hindered carbon (or SN1 for tertiary). Excess HI converts both halves to iodides.

Ethers that stand in air form explosive hydroperoxides by autoxidation (see the chapter on alkenes), so old bottles of diethyl ether and THF can be dangerous. **Crown ethers** are cyclic polyethers (18-crown-6) whose cavity binds a cation, K⁺ for 18-crown-6. They carry salts into organic solvents, leaving the anion bare and highly nucleophilic. Pedersen, Cram and Lehn shared the 1987 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for host–guest chemistry.

check.q: Why are ethers good solvents for Grignard reagents?
check.a: Their oxygen lone pairs coordinate to magnesium, and they have no acidic hydrogens
wrong: They react with the Grignard reagent

sections.title: Epoxides
body: An **epoxide** (oxirane) is a three-membered ring ether. Its 60° angles give about 115 kJ mol⁻¹ of ring strain, so, unlike other ethers, epoxides react readily with nucleophiles in ring opening. They are made by peroxyacid oxidation of alkenes (see the alkene chapter), or by treating a halohydrin with base (an intramolecular SN2). Ethylene oxide is made industrially by silver-catalyzed air oxidation of ethene, and converted to ethylene glycol (antifreeze, polyester) and to surfactants.
Ring opening follows two patterns, with opposite regiochemistry for an unsymmetrical epoxide:

head: Conditions
Mechanism
Nucleophile attacks
Example with propylene oxide
rows: Basic or neutral: RO⁻, HO⁻, RMgX, LiAlH₄, NH₃, CN⁻
Protonated epoxide; SN1-like with SN2 geometry
The more substituted carbon (more cationic character)
table.caption: Regiochemistry of epoxide opening.

body: In both cases the attack is from the back side, so the product has **anti** stereochemistry: opening a cyclohexene oxide with hydroxide or water gives a trans-1,2-diol. Epoxide opening by a Grignard reagent is a valuable two-carbon chain extension: R–MgBr + ethylene oxide gives R–CH₂CH₂–OH after workup.

example.title: Opening an unsymmetrical epoxide
example.problem: Give the product of 2,2-dimethyloxirane with (a) CH₃O⁻/CH₃OH and (b) CH₃OH/H₂SO₄.
solution: (a) Base: SN2 at the less hindered CH₂ carbon, giving (CH₃)₂C(OH)CH₂OCH₃ (1-methoxy-2-methylpropan-2-ol).
(b) Acid: the more substituted (tertiary) carbon bears more positive charge, so methanol attacks there, giving (CH₃)₂C(OCH₃)CH₂OH (2-methoxy-2-methylpropan-1-ol).

sections.title: Grignard, organolithium and organocuprate reagents
body: Carbon is normally electrophilic when bonded to a heteroatom. **Organometallic reagents** make it a nucleophile. A **Grignard reagent** forms when an alkyl or aryl halide reacts with magnesium metal in ether: R–Br + Mg → R–MgBr. An **organolithium** forms from R–X and 2 Li (or by deprotonation; n-butyllithium is a common base and nucleophile). The C–metal bond is highly polarized, so the carbon behaves like a **carbanion**, and these reagents are strong bases (conjugate acid pK_a about 50) and strong nucleophiles.

body.warn: Grignard and organolithium reagents are destroyed by any acidic hydrogen: water, alcohols, amines, terminal alkynes, carboxylic acids. They must be prepared and used in dry ether or THF under an inert atmosphere, and a substrate may not carry an O–H or N–H group (unless it is protected).

head: Electrophile
Product (after H₃O⁺ workup)
rows: Tertiary alcohol with two identical R groups
table.caption: Products of Grignard reagents with electrophiles.

body: Esters react twice: the first addition expels alkoxide to give a ketone, which is more reactive than the ester and adds a second equivalent. To stop at a ketone from an acid derivative, a less reactive reagent is needed.

**Organocuprates** (Gilman reagents, R₂CuLi) are made from two equivalents of RLi and CuI. They are softer, less basic nucleophiles. They couple with alkyl, vinyl and aryl halides (R₂CuLi + R′–X → R–R′), convert acid chlorides into ketones (they stop after one addition), and add in a conjugate (1,4) fashion to α,β-unsaturated ketones, whereas Grignard reagents usually add directly to the carbonyl (1,2).

example.title: Planning an alcohol synthesis
example.problem: Show two ways to make 2-phenylpropan-2-ol, PhC(CH₃)₂OH, from a Grignard reagent.
solution: The target is a tertiary alcohol with three different disconnection points: each of the three groups can be the Grignard carbon.
(1) PhMgBr + acetone. (2) CH₃MgBr + acetophenone. (3) CH₃MgBr (2 equiv.) + methyl benzoate.

Why can’t a Grignard reagent be prepared from 4-bromobutan-1-ol?
check.a: The O–H would protonate the reagent as it forms

sections.title: Thiols and sulfides
body: Sulfur lies below oxygen, and its compounds are analogues with different behavior. A **thiol** (R–SH) is more acidic than an alcohol (pK_a 10 against 16–18), and its conjugate base, the thiolate, is an excellent nucleophile and poor base, so thiolates give clean SN2 reactions with alkyl halides to form **sulfides** (thioethers). Thiols smell strongly (skunks, garlic, the odorant added to natural gas). Mild oxidation joins two thiols as a **disulfide**, R–S–S–R, and the reverse is a reduction. This S–S bond cross-links protein chains between cysteine residues, as in hair, and is why perming hair involves reduction and re-oxidation. Sulfides oxidize to **sulfoxides** (DMSO) and then **sulfones**.

check.q: What does mild oxidation of a thiol give?

wrong: Secondary, because the chain is branched
Tertiary, because it has a methyl branch near the OH
It cannot be classified because it is chiral
quiz.why: Classification counts the carbons attached to the carbinol carbon (the carbon bearing OH). That carbon, C1, has only one carbon neighbor, so the alcohol is primary no matter how branched the chain is elsewhere.

quiz.q: A compound contains both a ketone and an ethyl ester. It is treated with NaBH₄ in ethanol. What happens?
quiz.a: The ketone is reduced to a secondary alcohol and the ester is unchanged
wrong: Both the ketone and the ester are reduced
Only the ester is reduced, to a primary alcohol, because esters are more electrophilic than ketones
Neither is reduced, because NaBH₄ reduces only aldehydes and needs an acidic workup to touch a ketone
quiz.why: NaBH₄ is mild enough to reduce aldehydes and ketones but not esters or acids. LiAlH₄ would reduce both groups.

quiz.q: Four alcohols are shaken at room temperature with ZnCl₂ in concentrated HCl. Which becomes cloudy immediately?
quiz.why: The tertiary alcohol ionizes by SN1 almost at once to give the insoluble alkyl chloride. The secondary alcohols take minutes, and the primary alcohol does not react at room temperature.

quiz.q: (S)-Butan-2-ol is converted to its tosylate with TsCl and pyridine, and the tosylate is then treated with NaN₃. What is the configuration of the 2-azidobutane?
wrong: S, because inversion occurs in both steps and they cancel
S, because the nucleophile replaces the leaving group in the same position
quiz.why: Tosylate formation does not touch the C–O bond, so the configuration is retained. Azide then displaces tosylate by SN2 with one inversion. Azide and OH hold the same priority rank, so the label changes from S to R.

quiz.q: (R)-Octan-2-ol reacts with PPh₃, DEAD and benzoic acid. What is the configuration of the benzoate ester?
quiz.a: S, with inversion at the carbinol carbon
wrong: R, with retention, since the C–O bond is never broken
A racemic mixture, since the intermediate is a carbocation
No ester forms unless a carbodiimide is added
quiz.why: In the Mitsunobu reaction the oxygen is activated in place, and the carboxylate displaces it by SN2 from the back. Benzoate-O and OH have the same priority rank, so inversion changes R to S.

quiz.q: Butan-1-ol is treated with CrO₃ and H₂SO₄ in aqueous acetone (Jones reagent). What is the main product?
quiz.why: In water the aldehyde forms a hydrate, which is oxidized a second time. Stopping at the aldehyde would need anhydrous PCC or a Swern or Dess–Martin oxidation.

quiz.q: An orange solution of acidified dichromate is added to an unknown alcohol and slowly turns green. What can be concluded?
quiz.a: The alcohol has at least one hydrogen on its carbinol carbon, so it is primary or secondary
wrong: The solution changed color only because the dichromate was diluted by the alcohol
quiz.why: Orange Cr(VI) is reduced to green Cr(III) only when something is oxidized. A tertiary alcohol has no carbinol hydrogen and gives no reaction.

quiz.q: Pinacol, (CH₃)₂C(OH)C(OH)(CH₃)₂, is treated with NaIO₄. What is formed?
quiz.why: Periodate cleaves the bond between the two carbinol carbons of a 1,2-diol, giving a carbonyl compound from each. Pinacolone arises from pinacol under acid by a methyl shift, not from periodate.

quiz.q: Methyl tert-butyl ether is treated with one equivalent of cold HI. Which products are formed mainly?
wrong: No reaction, since ethers are inert to acids
quiz.why: After protonation of oxygen, the tertiary side leaves as a stable cation (SN1) and is captured by iodide. Backside SN2 on the hindered tertiary carbon is not possible.

quiz.q: Why does adding 18-crown-6 allow potassium fluoride to react in an organic solvent as a very strong nucleophile?
quiz.a: The crown ether wraps K⁺ in its cavity and carries the salt into solution, leaving the fluoride bare
wrong: The crown ether protonates fluoride to make HF
The crown ether reacts with the alkyl halide first and then delivers fluorine
The crown ether is a strong acid that dissolves the salt
quiz.why: A polyether cavity of the right size binds the cation. Without hydrogen bonding or ion pairing, the anion is highly nucleophilic.

quiz.q: Why can a bottle of THF that has stood open in air for years be dangerous?
wrong: THF polymerizes to a shock-sensitive solid on standing
THF hydrolyzes to butane-1,4-diol and pressure builds up
THF absorbs carbon dioxide and forms carbonates
quiz.why: Ethers react slowly with O₂ in a radical chain, giving hydroperoxides that can detonate when the solvent is concentrated or distilled.

quiz.q: 2,2-Dimethyloxirane reacts with NH₃ in ethanol (neutral or basic conditions). What is the major product?
quiz.why: Under basic or neutral conditions the nucleophile attacks the less hindered CH₂ carbon by SN2, leaving the oxygen on the tertiary carbon. Attack at the tertiary carbon is typical only under acid.

quiz.q: Cyclohexene oxide reacts with sodium methoxide in methanol. What is the product?
quiz.why: Methoxide attacks from the side opposite the epoxide oxygen, so the two groups end up on opposite faces of the ring (anti opening).

quiz.q: Ethylmagnesium bromide reacts with ethylene oxide, followed by H₃O⁺. What is the product?
quiz.why: The carbanion-like ethyl group attacks a CH₂ of the epoxide, adding two carbons to give CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH after protonation of the alkoxide.

quiz.q: Excess ethylmagnesium bromide reacts with methyl propanoate, then H₃O⁺. What is the product?
quiz.why: The first addition expels methoxide to give pentan-3-one, which is more reactive than the ester and adds a second ethyl group. The result is a tertiary alcohol with two identical added groups.

quiz.q: Cyclohex-2-en-1-one reacts with lithium dimethylcuprate, then H₃O⁺. What is the major product?
quiz.why: Gilman reagents add in a conjugate (1,4) fashion to α,β-unsaturated ketones. A Grignard reagent such as CH₃MgBr would give the 1,2-adduct, the allylic alcohol.

quiz.q: Which alkyl bromide cannot usefully be converted to its Grignard reagent with magnesium?
quiz.why: The terminal alkyne C–H (pK_a 25) is far more acidic than the conjugate acid of a Grignard carbon (about 50), so the reagent would protonate itself. The ether and aryl or alkyl halide are compatible.

quiz.q: Why is CH₃CH₂S⁻ a better choice than CH₃CH₂O⁻ for substitution on a secondary alkyl bromide?
quiz.a: Thiolate is a stronger nucleophile but a weaker base, so less E2 competes
wrong: Thiolate is a stronger base, so it is better at pulling the leaving group off the carbon
Alkoxide cannot act as a nucleophile at all
Thiolate is smaller than alkoxide, so it avoids steric hindrance at the secondary carbon
quiz.why: Sulfur is larger and more polarizable than oxygen, and RSH (pK_a about 10) is a stronger acid than ROH (16–18), so RS⁻ is the weaker base. Alkoxides do act as nucleophiles, but they also drive elimination.

summary: Alcohols come from alkene hydration, carbonyl reduction and Grignard additions. They are 1°, 2° or 3°, and phenols are much more acidic.
OH is made a leaving group through HX, SOCl₂ or PBr₃ (inversion), tosylation (retention, then SN2 inversion) or the Mitsunobu reaction (inversion).
Jones oxidation takes primary alcohols to acids, and PCC, Swern and Dess–Martin stop at aldehydes. Secondary alcohols give ketones.
Ethers are inert solvents, cleaved by HBr or HI. Epoxides open at the less hindered carbon with bases and at the more substituted carbon with acids, always anti.
Grignard and organolithium reagents are carbon nucleophiles and strong bases. They add to carbonyls and epoxides and require dry, aprotic conditions. Gilman reagents are softer and add 1,4.

problems.q: Give a synthesis of 3-methylhexan-3-ol from alkyl halides and carbonyl compounds, using any ketone, with a Grignard reagent.
problems.solution: 3-Methylhexan-3-ol is CH₃CH₂C(OH)(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃. Disconnecting any one of the three C–C bonds to the carbinol carbon gives a Grignard reagent and a ketone: (1) CH₃MgBr + hexan-3-one; (2) CH₃CH₂MgBr + pentan-2-one; (3) CH₃CH₂CH₂MgBr + butan-2-one.
problems.a: Any of the three ketone–Grignard combinations.

problems.q: Predict the products: (a) (S)-butan-2-ol + SOCl₂/pyridine; (b) cyclohexylmethanol + PCC; (c) cyclohexylmethanol + Na₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄/H₂O; (d) ethylene oxide + PhMgBr then H₃O⁺.
Explain the opposite regiochemistry of the reactions of methyloxirane with CH₃O⁻ and with CH₃OH/H⁺.
problems.solution: Methoxide attacks in an SN2 step, so it goes to the less hindered CH₂. Under acid the epoxide oxygen is protonated and the C–O bond to the more substituted carbon is weakened, so that carbon bears partial positive charge and is attacked by the weak nucleophile methanol.
problems.a: SN2 steric control (base) versus carbocation-like electronic control (acid).

problems.q: Show the retrosynthesis and forward synthesis of butanoic acid from 1-bromopropane.
problems.solution: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + Mg in ether gives CH₃CH₂CH₂MgBr. Add CO₂ (dry ice), then H₃O⁺: CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH.
